passage: At the village school parade, Charu stood in line with her hands behind her back, as Sir had taught, chin up. The flag went up, and the whole row stood the same way. Afterwards a peon told Charu that the headmaster wanted to see her. She stood outside his door, hands behind her back again, fingers tightly locked. Her friend Lavanya whispered, “Why are you hiding your hands? What did you do?” “Nothing!” said Charu, “I don't know why he called me.” The door opened. The headmaster was smiling. “Charu, your poem won the district prize.”

qa.q: What did the peon tell Charu after the parade?
qa.a: He told her that the headmaster wanted to see her.

qa.q: What might Charu's hands behind her back mean outside the door, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Probably nervousness, since her fingers were locked and she did not know why she was called. It could also be the parade habit of respect; it does not mean she had done something wrong.

qa.q: What would help Lavanya read the gesture better?
qa.a: Look at the context, the door and Charu's face, and ask kindly what is wrong instead of assuming guilt.

qa.q: How might Lavanya's question feel to Charu?
qa.a: It may have added to her worry, since she said she had done nothing. A gentler question would have felt more supportive.

grounding: Hands behind the back may signal respect, nervousness or concealment; it is not proof of guilt.

passage: On the school trip to the museum in Lagos, Emeka walked past the glass cases with his hands clasped behind his back. Wei, next to him, noticed and nudged him. “Why are your hands hidden? Did you take something?” Emeka rolled his eyes. “No. If I don't put them behind me, I'll touch things. Mum says I always do.” Wei laughed. The guide, who had overheard, smiled and said, “That's a good trick. The glass is there to protect the old pots.” Emeka kept his hands behind him and stared at the pots.

qa.q: Where was the school trip?
qa.a: The school trip was to the museum in Lagos.

qa.q: How might Emeka have felt when Wei asked if he had taken something?
qa.a: Probably a bit annoyed, since he rolled his eyes before explaining that he clasps his hands so he won't touch things.

qa.q: What did Wei do that helped, and what could he do next time?
qa.a: He asked Emeka directly and laughed, which cleared it up. Next time he could ask more gently before suggesting anything about taking things.

qa.q: How might the guide see Emeka's clasped hands?
qa.a: As a sensible way to avoid touching the old pots, and as respect for the exhibits.

grounding: Hands behind the back can signal respect or self-control; it is not proof of guilt.

passage: When the flower pot outside the staff room was found smashed, Uma Ma'am walked down the corridor asking questions. Tarun stood by the notice board with both hands behind his back, very still. Two children glanced at him. Uma Ma'am slowed. Hands hidden, standing stiff. It would have been easy to decide. Instead she asked, “Tarun, did you see what happened to the pot?” “No, Ma'am. I was in the library.” His ears were pink. “What are you holding?” He brought his hands round slowly: a folded card with glitter, “Happy Teachers' Day” on the front. “It was for tomorrow. It's a surprise.” Uma Ma'am's face softened.

qa.q: What was written on the front of the card?
qa.a: “Happy Teachers' Day” was written on the front.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling as he stood with his hands behind his back?
qa.a: He was probably nervous about being suspected, and also shy about his surprise card being found.

qa.q: Why was Uma Ma'am's approach fair?
qa.a: She didn't treat hidden hands as proof and asked plain questions, which revealed an innocent surprise.

qa.q: How might the two children who glanced at Tarun read his hands?
qa.a: They might have assumed he was hiding something to do with the broken pot, since hidden hands can look guilty.

grounding: Shows a child's hands behind the back signalling concealment of something innocent, and why the pose is not proof of guilt.

passage: I'm Payal. At the Independence Day parade, Pema stood in front of me in the line, hands clasped behind her back, chin up, feet apart, exactly as the PT teacher showed us. She looked proud. On Monday I saw her again, outside the principal's office, and her hands were behind her back again. But this time her fingers were twisting together, and she kept shifting from one foot to the other. The office helper said, “What has she done?” I said I didn't know. Later she told me she'd been called in to hear she'd won the essay prize. Same hands. Totally different Pema.

qa.q: Where did Payal see Pema on Monday?
qa.a: Payal saw Pema outside the principal's office.

qa.q: What was Pema likely feeling outside the principal's office?
qa.a: She was likely nervous, twisting her fingers and shifting her feet, not knowing why she'd been called.

qa.q: What lesson could the office helper take from this?
qa.a: That hands behind the back don't prove someone has done something wrong, and waiting to find out is fairer.

qa.q: How does Payal compare the two poses?
qa.a: Payal notices that the same hands meant pride at the parade but nerves outside the office, shown by the twisting fingers and shifting feet.

grounding: Shows a child's hands behind the back meaning respect at a parade and nervousness elsewhere, and not proof of guilt.

passage: Saturday: Harish arrived at Vandana Dadi's house and stood in the doorway, hands locked behind his back. Dadi frowned. “What have you broken this time?” “Nothing!” His face went red. Sunday: At the temple, when the priest spoke to him, Harish stood the same way, hands behind, back straight. Dadi watched. It was how the school made them stand for assembly, Papa explained. Just manners. Dadi felt a small pinch of guilt about Saturday. Tuesday: Harish came in with his hands behind his back again. Dadi only smiled and waited. He held out a jar of tamarind sweets. “Your favourite,” he said, grinning.

qa.q: Where did Harish stand the same way on Sunday?
qa.a: At the temple, when the priest spoke to him.

qa.q: What was Dadi feeling after Papa's explanation on Sunday?
qa.a: Dadi felt a small pinch of guilt about accusing Harish on Saturday, realising the pose was manners.

qa.q: What did Dadi do differently on Tuesday, and why was it better?
qa.a: She smiled and waited instead of assuming he had broken something, which let the surprise gift come out.

qa.q: How might Harish have felt when Dadi asked what he'd broken?
qa.a: He likely felt hurt and embarrassed, since he'd done nothing and was only standing politely.

grounding: Shows a child's hands behind the back meaning respect, then a surprise, and a grandparent learning it is not proof of guilt.

passage: "Tanuja, you stand with your hands behind your back just like I did at school parade. That was how we showed respect. But let me, your Shalini Mami, tell you about the day it got me into trouble. The class chalk box had gone missing. I was standing at the back with my hands behind me, twisting my fingers. Our teacher marched over. 'What are you hiding?' Everyone turned. I was hiding something: my hands were blue to the wrist from a leaking pen, and I was ashamed. Slowly I showed her. She looked, and her face changed. She said sorry in front of everyone. The chalk turned up in the cupboard. Hands behind your back can mean many things, child."

qa.q: Why were young Shalini's hands blue?
qa.a: They were blue to the wrist from a leaking pen.

qa.q: What was young Shalini feeling while twisting her fingers behind her back?
qa.a: Ashamed and nervous about her ink-stained hands, not guilty about the chalk; the hidden hands looked like concealment but were embarrassment.

qa.q: What could the teacher in the story have done differently at the start?
qa.a: Asked quietly, without assuming guilt in front of the whole class, since hands behind the back are not proof of anything.

qa.q: How might the teacher have felt when she saw the blue hands?
qa.a: She likely felt embarrassed and sorry for accusing Shalini in front of everyone, which is why her face changed and she apologised.

grounding: It is an elder's memory of hands behind the back being read as hiding stolen chalk when they meant embarrassment, showing it is not proof of guilt.
